\(A\) takes up two moles of \(H_{2}\) to give decalin, so \(A\) is a bicyclic \(C_{10}H_{14}\) with the decalin carbon skeleton and two \(C=C\) bonds. The oxidative cleavage products fix where those double bonds sit: cyclohexane-1,2-dicarboxylic acid keeps a six-membered ring intact and carries two \(COOH\) groups on adjacent carbons, while the second fragment is oxalic acid (a two-carbon dicarboxylic acid). Counting carbons, \(6+2\) ring-plus-carboxyl carbons \(+2\) from oxalic acid \(=10\).
That pattern requires one ring to be fully saturated and the other to carry a conjugated diene at the two positions away from the ring fusion, i.e. double bonds between C5-C6 and C7-C8 of an octahydronaphthalene. Cleaving both gives \(COOH\) on each ring-fusion carbon (from C5 and C8) - the cyclohexane-1,2-dicarboxylic acid - while the intact C6-C7 bond becomes \(HOOC-COOH\).
The other options fail: a structure with one \(C=C\) in each ring (options A and B) has both rings opened on cleavage and gives a single acyclic tetracarboxylic acid, and a structure with a double bond at the ring fusion (option D) destroys both rings as well. Hence C.

Heating a carboxylic acid with aqueous ammonia first gives the ammonium salt, which loses water on strong heating to give the amide. Treating an amide with \(Br_{2}\) and \(KOH\) is the Hofmann bromamide degradation, which removes the carbonyl carbon as carbonate and gives a primary amine with one carbon fewer.
Working back from the amine: only benzoic acid \(\rightarrow\) benzamide \(\rightarrow\) aniline is internally consistent. Aniline is \(C_{6}H_{7}N\), matching the seven hydrogens and one nitrogen quoted in the stem.
The other options break the carbon count or the chemistry: benzoic acid cannot give 4-methylbenzamide (option C); \(p\)-toluic acid would give 4-methylaniline, not 2-methylaniline (option B); and phenylethanoic acid would give benzylamine, whose skeleton does not match a simple Hofmann product sequence quoted here (option D). Answer A.

\(C_{6}H_{12}O_{3}\) has one degree of unsaturation, so only one carbonyl can be present; the other two oxygens must be ether-type. \(P\) gives iodoform but not Tollens' test, so it contains a methyl ketone and no free aldehyde. Dilute acid converts \(P\) to \(Q\), and \(Q\) now answers both tests - so acid hydrolysis has unmasked an aldehyde. That is the signature of an acetal.
Hence \(P=CH_{3}COCH_{2}CH(OCH_{3})_{2}\): the dimethyl acetal of 3-oxobutanal. Formula check: \(C_{4}\) chain \(+\) two \(OCH_{3}\) \(=C_{6}\); \(H=3+2+1+6=12\); \(O=1+2=3\). Hydrolysis gives \(Q=CH_{3}COCH_{2}CHO\), which has both a methyl ketone (iodoform positive) and an aldehyde (Tollens positive).
The others fail: the option with two isolated \(OCH_{3}\) ethers is not hydrolysed by dilute acid; the option written with a free \(CHO\) would make \(P\) itself Tollens positive; and the acetal of a diketone hydrolyses to butane-2,3-dione, which has no aldehyde and so fails Tollens. Answer B.

All four are canonical (resonance) structures of the same nitro-substituted \(C_{4}\) system, so stability is judged by the usual rules: minimise charge separation, keep octets, put negative charge on the more electronegative atom, and above all never place like charges on adjacent atoms.
Option C is \(CH_{2}=CH-\overset{-}{C}H-\overset{+}{C}H-\overset{+}{N}(=O)(O^{-})\). Its carbocation sits directly on the carbon bonded to the already positive nitrogen, so two positive centres are adjacent - the strongest destabilising feature available. In addition the adjacent carbanion and carbocation should simply collapse to a \(\pi\) bond, and the positive carbon is not stabilised by the alkene (it is not allylic in this arrangement).
By contrast, option D places the negative charge on the carbon next to the positive nitrogen (opposite charges adjacent, favourable) with the positive charge allylic to the alkene; option B keeps the nitro group in its normal form with an allyl-type cation; and option A, although it carries four formal charges, has the positive carbon allylic and both negative charges on the electronegative oxygens with no like charges adjacent.
Least stable is therefore option C.
